Environmental Ed Day 15 Poetry Slam

Nov 2, 2010 • Janice Cotcher

Today in my enviro ed class, we explored the idea of using poetry slam and podcasts with students. Certainly not an easy thing to do. My first attempt at a poetry slam (Sorry, I was unable to load the mp3 file of my poetry slam so the text will have to do.):

Wasted space, wasted water Keeping up with the Joneses Manicured lawns and colourful flower beds yet nothing to feed you Chemicals, water, controlling nature

I find the idea of turf farms very strange Rows and rows of grass harvested and then transplanted into an ecosystem that cannot naturally support it. All for the sake for the ideal yard. I thought beautiful yards were for the wealthy. For those with so much land that produces so much food that they can afford the pretend pastoral life. All these people making themselves poor pretending to be wealthy.

I saw a story about how the city of Las Vegas was paying home owners to rip up their lawn. Grass in the desert? This is the land of sand and cacti reaching high to the sky and low in the ground just to find a precious and rare resource only to save it for another day. A city causing drought by consuming water for grass. I heard that money was offered but refused because no one wanted to give up their green space.

How silly are we to tear up natural grasslands to transplant blue-green grass that belongs in Kentucky with its humid subtropics. What happened to the hardy grass of the prairie? Why do we not plant this? I’ve been told its a fire hazard.

To cleanse your mind from my lameness check out my favorite poetry slam, Taylor Mali on “What Teachers Make” (viewer discretion is advised):

I think a poetry slam would be an excellent way for students to express their anger/ fears/frustration over environmental issues. In our class we used to program GarageBand to record our poetry as a podcast. Instead of reading our work in front of the class, we played the podcast from our computer. It took away some of the performance anxiety to be able to not have to read it live. GarageBand also lets you change your voice so then students could share their poetry anonymously. Now I just have to think of a way to fit this into my teaching…
